blocks.heading: What’s This?
paragraphs: When you begin learning Arabic, one of the first things I want you to do is start learning about the world around you—but while using proper grammar from the very beginning.

Think of it as if you were an infant again. You would not begin with complicated ideas or long conversations. You would look at the people and objects around you, notice something unfamiliar, and begin asking simple questions: “What’s this?” “What’s that?” and “What is that called?”

That is where I want you to begin. Instead of simply memorizing random lists of words, you are going to learn how to ask about what you see, understand the answers you receive, and use those new words in short, complete sentences.

This question gives you a practical way to interact with Arabic from the very beginning. You can use it while pointing to something in a shop, asking your teacher about a new word, looking around someone’s home, reading a sign, or trying to understand something you notice on the street.

Throughout this chapter, you will use this question to identify and describe the people, places, and things around you. You will learn the grammar gradually—not as a collection of abstract rules, but as a tool that helps you talk about what you actually see and say what you mean.

You will also hear Jordanian and Palestinian speakers ask these questions in slightly different ways. Do not worry about learning every variation right now. Each form and pattern will be introduced gradually. For now, your goal is to begin recognizing the patterns, asking questions, and listening carefully to the answers.
Real conversations move forward through questions. The more questions you can ask, the more opportunities you create to hear Arabic, understand it, and begin using it for yourself.
يعني comes from the verb meaning “to mean.” As a verb form, it can mean “he/it means,” but in everyday conversation it is also a filler word that never changes.

In Levantine Arabic, you are going to hear يعني all the time. It stays يعني no matter who is speaking. Rather than overcomplicate it, let’s look at it together and see how people actually use it in a few common situations.

blocks.heading: 1. As a Filler
paragraphs: People often use يعني the way English speakers use “like,” “you know,” or “I mean.” It can give you a moment to think, soften what you are saying, or place a little more emphasis on your point.

blocks.heading: 2. As a Clarifier
paragraphs: You can also use يعني to explain what a statement means or implies. In this situation, it works like “meaning,” “in other words,” or “that is.”

items.translit: il-bēt ẓghīr, yaʿni mish munāsib ilna.
items.en: “The house is small, meaning it isn’t suitable for us.”

blocks.heading: 3. Asking a Question
paragraphs: If someone uses a word you do not recognize or says something you do not understand, you can use يعني to ask for clarification. This is one of the most useful questions you can learn as a beginner:

items.en: “What does that mean?” / “What do you mean?”

lines.speaker: A
lines.ar: سَيّارْتي الجْديدة حِلوة، يَعني حِلوة كتير
lines.translit: sayyārtī il-jdīde ḥilwe, yaʿni ḥilwe ktīr
lines.en: My new car is pretty—like, really pretty.

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: What do you mean pretty? It’s ordinary.

blocks.heading: Vocabulary AS A MEDITATION
paragraphs: Learning vocabulary becomes easier when you have a dependable system. Instead of memorizing a word once and hoping it stays with you, build a routine that helps you hear it, understand it, remember it, and use it again.

Throughout this book, you will encounter many new Arabic nouns. This is intentional. Nouns give you the vocabulary to describe people, places, objects, and ideas, and you will return to these words as you learn new grammatical structures.
You do not need to memorize every word immediately. Focus on recognizing words, practicing their pronunciation, and gradually recalling them without looking at the English translation.

blocks.heading: Turn Your Practice into a Meditation
paragraphs: Vocabulary practice does not need to feel rushed or stressful. Set aside a few minutes, remove distractions, and focus on one word or expression at a time. Say it aloud, picture what it represents, and repeat it at a comfortable pace.
The goal is consistent, focused practice rather than perfect memorization.

blocks.heading: Introducing the Sound–Image–Feeling Loop
paragraphs: One method I recommend is the Sound–Image–Feeling Loop (SIFL). The idea is to connect the sound of an Arabic word with a mental image and a meaningful association, rather than relying exclusively on English translation.
On the following page, we will explore how to use this method.
Remember, SIFL is one option, not a requirement. Flashcards, speaking practice, listening, and other methods can also help. The best system is one you can use consistently.

blocks.heading: 2.1 The Noun — il-ism | الاسم
paragraphs: Let me give you a fair warning: for much of this book, we are heading back to elementary school grammar. We are starting with one of the most basic building blocks of language: the noun.
A noun is simply a word that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Words like these are all nouns:
These are the people, places, things, and ideas we talk about every day. Nouns give us the who and the what of what we want to say, which makes them a natural place to begin building your Arabic.
In the vocabulary bank at the start of this chapter, you saw many of the nouns we will use throughout this chapter, with their plural forms included alongside the singular forms.
You are not expected to memorize all of these plurals right now.

In terms of meaning and use, plurals work much as they do in English: one book becomes several books, one city becomes several cities, and so on. What may feel unfamiliar is how Arabic forms those plurals. For now, I want you to learn the words before the rules.

Throughout this book, you will encounter singular and plural forms together. Rather than memorizing all the rules for forming plurals immediately, begin by recognizing and using these forms as vocabulary.

Some plurals follow predictable patterns, while others involve changes within the word itself. These are often called broken plurals. You do not need to master these patterns yet. For now, practice the forms you encounter and begin noticing similarities between them.

blocks.heading: Gender — الجنس | il-jins
paragraphs: In English, grammatical gender is limited, and words like he and she usually refer to people. Arabic works differently. Every noun is classified as either masculine or feminine, whether it refers to a person, animal, place, or object.
For example, a boy is masculine, but so is a book. A girl is feminine, but so is a car. Even words borrowed from other languages are assigned a grammatical gender.
This distinction matters because pronouns, adjectives, and demonstratives often change to agree with the noun they refer to. Learning a noun therefore means learning its gender as well.

blocks.heading: Masculine Nouns
paragraphs: Masculine is generally the unmarked/default form in the patterns you will learn first. If a noun does not have a clear feminine marker, it is usually treated as masculine.
These nouns do not have a special feminine ending, so they are masculine.

blocks.heading: Feminine Nouns
paragraphs: Most feminine nouns are easy to recognize because they end in tāʾ marbūṭa (ة).
In everyday Levantine Arabic, this ending is usually pronounced -e or -a. When another ending is attached, such as a possessive suffix, the ة is pronounced as t. We will return to this change later.
Notice the pattern: each of these feminine nouns ends in ة.

From this point forward, make a habit of noticing whether every new noun is masculine or feminine. This is not an optional detail. Gender affects many of the structures you will build throughout the language.

blocks.heading: A Few Exceptions
paragraphs: The tāʾ marbūṭa (ة) is a strong clue that a noun is feminine, but it is not an absolute rule. Some masculine nouns also end in ة.
Although زلمة ends in ة, it is grammatically masculine.
Exceptions like this are relatively uncommon. For now, you can generally assume that nouns ending in ة are feminine unless you learn otherwise.

blocks.heading: Feminine Without a Marker
paragraphs: Not every feminine noun ends in tāʾ marbūṭa (ة). Some feminine nouns have no visible feminine ending at all. Many of these are natural forces, body parts, or places, but others, such as حَرْب (war), simply have to be learned. ناس (people) is a special case: it often takes feminine singular agreement, but plural agreement is also common.

These nouns must be learned individually because their feminine gender is not indicated by a visible ending. Fortunately, many are common words that you will encounter repeatedly, making their gender easier to remember through practice.

blocks.heading: Gender in Action
paragraphs: To make this concrete, notice how the adjective “big” changes:
Same adjective, different ending. This pattern runs through the entire language.

blocks.heading: The Main Rules to Remember
blocks.text: Masculine is the default. If a noun ends in a tāʾ marbūṭa (ة), it is almost always feminine. If a noun has no marker at all but is still feminine, you have to learn it that way. Those three facts will carry you a long way.

blocks.heading: Definiteness: The Specific vs. the General
paragraphs: In English, words like “a” and “the” help us distinguish between something general and something specific. If you ask for “a book,” any book will do. If you ask for “the book,” you mean one particular book that both you and the listener already have in mind. In grammar, this distinction is called definiteness.
A noun used by itself is generally indefinite in Levantine Arabic. That is, a noun by itself generally carries the sense of “a” or “an” unless something makes it specific.
Take a look at these indefinite nouns:
Each noun is standing on its own, so each one is indefinite: a house, a book, a girl. So how does a noun become definite?

blocks.heading: Definiteness
paragraphs: There are several ways a noun can become definite in Arabic. For now, we will focus on three of the most common: the definite article الـ, possessive suffixes, and proper nouns.
Although these structures work differently, they share one important feature: each allows us to identify a particular person, place, or thing.
Let’s look at them one at a time.

blocks.heading: 1. The Definite Article
paragraphs: The first way is the most familiar. Arabic uses ال (il-) in much the same way English uses the. It attaches directly to the noun and tells us that we are talking about something specific.
Simply adding ال changes the noun from general to specific.

blocks.heading: 2. Possession
paragraphs: The second way a noun can become definite is through possession. This idea is not completely new. You actually used possession back in Chapter 1 when you learned how to ask someone’s name:
Look closely at اسم (ism), meaning name:
The endings ـي (-ī) and ـك (-ak) tell us who the noun belongs to. These are called possessive suffixes, and they attach directly to the noun.
Possession also makes a noun definite. Think about the difference between a house and my house. A house could be any house. My house identifies a specific one.
The same idea works in Arabic:

items.note: ¹ Note: When a feminine noun ending in ة takes a possessive suffix, the ة becomes ت in both writing and pronunciation. We will look at this change more closely later in the chapter.

paragraphs: Because the possessive suffix already makes the noun definite, you do not add الـ (il-):
We will learn the full system of possessive suffixes later in this chapter. For now, remember the basic contrast:
The first is indefinite. The other two are definite, but they become definite in different ways.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text: A noun that is already definite through possession does not take الـ.

blocks.heading: 3. Proper Nouns
paragraphs: There is one more important way a noun can be definite: by being a proper noun.
A proper noun is the name of a specific person, place, or thing. You've already been using these, too.
When you say:
The names أحمد and فاطمة are already definite because they function as names identifying particular people. They do not need the definite article الـ.
The same principle applies to place names, although some place names already contain الـ as part of their established form.

blocks.heading: A Quick Note: Proper Nouns and Gender
paragraphs: Here's something important to remember: proper nouns have grammatical gender, just like other Arabic nouns.
When talking about people, the gender of a name is usually straightforward. But what about cities?
In Arabic, city names are generally treated as grammatically feminine, even when they don't end in ة (tāʾ marbūṭa).
Take عمّان (ʿAmmān), the capital of Jordan, for example.
Notice that we use كْبيرة (kbīre), the feminine form of the adjective, even though عمّان doesn't have a visible feminine ending.
The important thing to remember is that a noun doesn't need to end in ة to be feminine. Some nouns, including city names, are feminine simply because of how Arabic classifies them.
Keep this in mind as you work through the next drill!

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
A noun can become definite in three ways:
1. The definite article: the house – il-bēt | البيت
2. Possession: my house – bētī | بيتي
3. A proper noun: Ahmad – Aḥmad | أحمد
The result is the same each time: the noun refers to something specific.

blocks.heading: SPECIAL NOTE: Sun Letters — حروف الشمس | ḥurūf ish-shams
paragraphs: Arabic has 14 consonants known as sun letters. When the definite article الـ (il-) comes before one of these letters, the ل (lām) is not pronounced. Instead, the first consonant of the noun is doubled in pronunciation. This process is called assimilation.
The spelling of الـ does not change. Only its pronunciation changes.
There are 14 sun letters:
ت، ث، د، ذ، ر، ز، س، ش، ص، ض، ط، ظ، ل، ن
t, th, d, dh, r, z, s, sh, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ, l, n

These consonants are produced at or near the front of the mouth, relatively close to where l is formed. This helps explain why the l of the definite article naturally assimilates into the following sound. Many speakers also treat ج as a sun letter (ij-jār), but this book writes il-j.
Take the word شمس (shams), meaning sun. When we add the definite article الـ (il-), we write:
The ل is still there in writing, but it is not pronounced. Instead, the sh sound is doubled:
il- + shams → ish-shams
The same pattern applies whenever الـ comes before a sun letter.
All remaining Arabic letters are called moon letters. Before a moon letter, the l in il- is pronounced normally:

blocks.heading: Key Rule
blocks.text:
The spelling never changes: the definite article is always written الـ.
Only the pronunciation changes:
Before a sun letter: do not pronounce the ل; double the following consonant instead.
Before a moon letter: pronounce the ل normally.

lessons.title: Demonstrative Pronouns — asmāʾ il-ishāra | أسماء الإشارة

blocks.heading: 2.2 Demonstrative Pronouns — asmāʾ il-ishāra | أسماء الإشارة
paragraphs: Demonstratives are pointing words—the Arabic equivalents of this, that, these, and those. You already know that definiteness helps distinguish something general from something specific. Demonstratives work directly with that idea: they allow you to point out exactly which person or thing you mean.
When a demonstrative directly modifies a noun—as in this book or that car—the noun is definite and takes الـ (il-):
But there is an important distinction. If the noun after the demonstrative is indefinite, you are no longer saying this book or that car. You are forming a complete nominal sentence:
For now, pay close attention to whether the noun has the definite article الـ. This small difference changes the grammatical structure.

blocks.heading: This and That: Singular Forms
paragraphs: Southern Levantine Arabic has different singular demonstratives depending on gender and distance.

blocks.heading: Near Forms
paragraphs: هادا (hāda) and هاي (hāy) are the near forms. Use them when something is close to you—something you are holding, pointing to nearby, or talking about in the immediate situation.
In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, these forms can sometimes cover both English this and that, with context making the intended meaning clear.

items.note: 1 Note: In Southern Levantine Arabic, هادا (hāda) and هاد (hād) are two common forms of the masculine singular demonstrative. This book generally uses hāda, but you will hear hād frequently in natural speech. There is no difference in meaning between them.

blocks.heading: Far Forms
paragraphs: هداك (hadāk) and هديك (hadīk) are the far forms. Use them when pointing to something farther away or referring to something more distant in the conversation.
With singular nouns, gender matters. Use the masculine demonstratives hāda / hād and hadāk with masculine nouns, and the feminine demonstratives hāy and hadīk with feminine nouns.

blocks.heading: These and Those: Plural Forms
paragraphs: Arabic also has plural demonstratives corresponding to English these and those. The good news is that the plural forms do not change for masculine and feminine nouns. The same forms are used with all plural nouns.
The same basic near/far distinction applies:

blocks.heading: A Common Spoken Form: هالـ
paragraphs: There is another form you will hear constantly in everyday Levantine Arabic: هالـ (hal-/ha-).
When هالـ comes directly before a noun, it can express the idea of this or these without requiring a separate masculine or feminine demonstrative. It attaches directly to the noun:
Notice something useful: هالـ does not change for gender. You can use the same form before a masculine or feminine noun:
It can also be used with plural nouns:
The noun remains definite. In everyday speech, هالـ functions as a very common demonstrative form attached directly to the noun.

You should still learn hāda, hāy, hadōl, hadāk, hadīk, and hadōlāk. You will need them when the demonstrative stands on its own, when you want to distinguish near from far, and in many other common sentence patterns.
For now, simply begin recognizing هالـ as another very common way Levantine speakers point to a specific person or thing.

blocks.heading: Key Rule
blocks.text:
Plural demonstratives do not distinguish between masculine and feminine.
For now, keep the pattern simple:
Near → hadōl | هدول
Far → hadōlāk | هدولاك
Arabic plurals behave differently from English plurals in several important ways, and we will study those differences in Volume Two. For now, focus on recognizing and using hadōl for things that are nearby and hadōlāk for things that are farther away.
You will continue seeing both forms in examples and drills, giving you plenty of time to become comfortable with them before we study plurals in greater detail.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
Demonstratives help your listener identify exactly which person or thing you mean:
a book – ktāb | كتاب ↓
the book – il-ktāb | الكتاب ↓
this book – hāda il-ktāb | هادا الكتاب
The noun goes from general → definite → specifically pointed out.

blocks.heading: 2.3 The Adjective — iṣ-ṣifa | الصفة
paragraphs: An adjective is a describing word. If a noun gives us the label—house, girl, car—the adjective gives us the detail: big, beautiful, new. Adjectives tell us more about a noun’s color, size, quality, or even feeling. Without adjectives, we can name the world around us, but we cannot say very much about it.

In English, an adjective generally stays the same regardless of the noun it describes. Take the adjective “big,” for example: a big boy, big girls, the big house. The word big stays exactly the same each time.

Arabic works differently. An adjective must match the noun it describes. This is called agreement, and it is one of the most important features of Arabic grammar. A feminine noun takes a feminine adjective, a masculine noun takes a masculine adjective, and a plural noun requires the appropriate plural form. The adjective also changes depending on whether the noun is definite or indefinite.
In other words, an adjective mirrors its noun in three important ways: gender, number, and definiteness. We will work through each one in turn.

blocks.heading: Word Order
paragraphs: Before we get into agreement, there is one fundamental difference from English to establish: in Arabic, the adjective comes after the noun, not before it.
English: adjective + noun — big house, beautiful girl, new car
Arabic: noun + adjective — house big, girl beautiful, car new
This noun-first order is consistent throughout the language. Once it becomes automatic, it will feel natural — but it takes deliberate practice at first.

blocks.heading: Gender — الجنس | il-jins
paragraphs: As we discussed with nouns, Arabic is a gendered language: every noun is either masculine or feminine. Because of this, adjectives must agree with the noun in gender.
In English, adjectives do not change form. In Arabic, however, the adjective changes depending on the gender of the noun it describes.
How It Works:
•  Masculine noun → use the masculine form of the adjective (base form, no special ending)
•  Feminine noun → use the feminine form of the adjective (usually ends in -e / -a; for nisba adjectives, -iyye)

blocks.title: Gender Association Drill
blocks.instructions:
Instructions: Read each noun aloud and choose the pronoun that matches its grammatical gender: هو (huwwe) for masculine or هي (hiyye) for feminine. Use the same pronouns for people and objects.
First, work slowly and take your time. Say the noun, then its matching pronoun. Write the pronoun in the blank.
Then repeat the drill aloud. Gradually work toward looking at each word and immediately saying the right pronoun. The goal is to encode the connection so that the noun brings its gender to mind automatically.
Example: bēt → huwwe | بيت ← هو 
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.heading: Definiteness — التعريف | it-taʿrīf
paragraphs: When a noun and an adjective form one noun–adjective combination, the adjective must match the noun not only in gender, but also in definiteness.
If the noun is indefinite, the adjective must also be indefinite. Neither word takes الـ.
If the noun is definite, the adjective must also be definite.
When a noun becomes definite through the article الـ, both the noun and the adjective take الـ.
But remember: The definite article الـ is not the only way to make a noun definite.
You have already learned that possessive endings and proper names can also make nouns definite.
For example:
Notice that بَيْتي is already definite because of the possessive ending ـي (my). We do not add الـ to the noun. However, the adjective still takes الـ because it must match the noun's definiteness.
The pattern is:
Indefinite noun + indefinite adjective
Definite noun + definite adjective
The important point is that the adjective must match the noun's definiteness, regardless of how that noun becomes definite.
Be careful: If a definite noun is followed by an indefinite adjective, as in البَيْت كْبير, the words no longer mean “the big house.” Instead, they mean “The house is big.”
This is a different construction, which you will learn shortly.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
Whenever you are building a noun–adjective combination, remember that the adjective must match the noun in both gender and definiteness.
A definite noun requires a definite adjective, even when the noun itself does not have الـ.

blocks.heading: The Archetype Adjective Pattern — فعيل | faʿīl
paragraphs: Now we are going to look at two very common adjective types. These are not the only adjective patterns in Arabic, but they are among the most useful, and they will help you begin recognizing how Arabic adjectives are formed.

The first type includes adjectives such as كبير (kbīr), صغير (ẓghīr), and فقير (faʾīr). Many adjectives of this type are built around the pattern فعيل (faʿīl), one of the most common descriptive patterns in Arabic. I call this the Archetype Pattern.

blocks.heading: Note
blocks.text: فعيل (faʿīl) is not a vocabulary word that you would use by itself. The letters ف–ع–ل are placeholders that show us where the consonants and vowels fit within a family of words.

paragraphs: Do not worry—I am not asking you to master Arabic roots and patterns yet. For now, I simply want you to notice the rhythm of the pattern and begin training your ear to recognize it. We will explore how Arabic roots fit into different patterns in much greater depth in Volume Two.

What should you notice? The clearest marker is the long ī sound before the final consonant. The complete pattern is faʿīl, which you can hear clearly in faʾīr. In everyday Levantine speech, however, the first short vowel may disappear. That is why words such as kabīr and ṣaghīr are commonly pronounced kbīr and ẓghīr. Even when that first vowel drops, the long ī remains.

Arabic is full of patterns like this. Later, we will look closely at how three-consonant roots fit into different patterns to produce different kinds of words. For now, going too deeply into that system would only distract us from what we are trying to learn. At this stage, I simply want you to recognize the sound.
To form the feminine, adjectives of this type usually add a tāʾ marbūṭa (ة). In Levantine Arabic, this ending is typically pronounced -e:

blocks.heading: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Many common masculine adjectives follow the faʿīl pattern and form the feminine by adding -e (ـة). In everyday speech, the first short vowel may disappear, but the long ī usually remains easy to hear.

blocks.title: Noun + Adjective Drill
blocks.instructions:
Instructions: In each item, the noun is already provided in Arabic and transliteration. Your job is to complete the phrase by adding the correct form of the adjective in both blanks.
This may seem simple, but it is one of the most important patterns in Arabic. Before completing each phrase, remember three things:
The adjective comes after the noun.
The gender must match: a masculine noun takes a masculine adjective, and a feminine noun takes a feminine adjective.
The definiteness must match. In this drill, nouns without الـ are indefinite, so their adjectives do not take الـ either. When a noun has الـ, its adjective must also have الـ.
Remember that nouns can also become definite through possession, even without الـ. We will practice those combinations later.
Say every completed phrase out loud—and repeat it. Repetition is your friend! We will build on this with more drills later so that the pattern becomes firmly encoded and eventually feels automatic.

blocks.heading: The Nisba Adjective Pattern — النسبة | in-nisba
paragraphs: The second type is the Nisba Pattern. A nisba adjective expresses connection or relationship. It tells you that something is related to, comes from, or belongs to something else—such as a place, identity, field of study, or concept.

The key feature of the nisba is the ending -ī. This sound signals meanings like “related to,” “from,” or “belonging to.” Essentially, we are taking a noun and turning it into an adjective that shows connection.

English does something similar by adding -y. For example: taste → tasty, health → healthy, rain → rainy. Arabic works in much the same way, even with a similar sounding ending ī (written -i at the end of a word, where it is said short: amrīki, but amrīkiyye). When the nisba is feminine, it adds ـة, which in Levantine is pronounced -iyye.

lessons.title: The WDGN System — The Bridge to Sentences

blocks.heading: WDGN System — The Bridge to Sentences
paragraphs: Learning to pair nouns and adjectives correctly is one of the first steps toward building real sentences in Arabic. In the beginning, however, I do not want you to rush through the drills or simply guess what sounds right. I encourage my students to slow down and run each phrase through a simple mental checklist.

The goal is not for you to rely on this checklist forever. Once you have enough experience with the language, these patterns will begin to come out naturally, and you will no longer need to think through every step. In the beginning, though, the checklist helps make sure that everything comes out correctly. More importantly, it helps you encode the proper patterns from the start so that you are repeatedly practicing the correct structure.
The mental checklist I use with my students is called WDGN. It covers the four things you should check whenever an adjective directly modifies a noun:
W — Word Order: Does the adjective come after the noun?
D — Definiteness: Does the adjective match the noun in definiteness?
G — Gender: Does the adjective match the noun in gender?
N — Number: Does the adjective match the noun in number?

As you work through the early drills, take your time and check each point in order. At first, this process may feel slow and deliberate—that is perfectly fine. Each correct repetition helps train your brain to recognize and reproduce the pattern. Eventually, you will stop consciously running through the checklist because the correct structure will begin to feel natural.

blocks.heading: W — Word Order
paragraphs: In English, the adjective comes before the noun: a new car, a tall man. In Arabic, the order is reversed — the noun always comes first, and the adjective follows it.
This is one of the most fundamental adjustments you will make as a learner. It feels unnatural at first, but with enough repetition it becomes second nature.

blocks.heading: D — Definiteness
paragraphs: Definiteness spreads across the entire noun phrase. If the noun takes il-, the adjective must also take il-. If the noun is indefinite, the adjective stays indefinite too.
A noun with a possessive suffix is also definite. Although the possessed noun does not take il-, the adjective describing it still does.

blocks.heading: REMEMBER
blocks.text:
When an adjective directly describes a noun, it must match that noun in definiteness.
A definite noun followed by an adjective without il- can form a complete nominal sentence rather than a descriptive phrase. We will explore this distinction shortly.

blocks.heading: G — Gender
paragraphs: Every Arabic noun is either masculine or feminine, and the adjective must match. This is one of the most important habits to build early, because gender agreement runs through nearly everything in the language.

Masculine nouns take the masculine form of the adjective. Feminine nouns take the feminine form, which typically adds the tāʾ marbūṭa ending (-e / -a) — the same marker you already know from feminine nouns.
Notice that the adjective ending is the only thing that changes — the root stays the same. Once you know the masculine form of an adjective, the feminine is almost always predictable.

blocks.heading: N — Number
paragraphs: Number is the last part of WDGN, but plural agreement requires a little more care.
With people, a plural noun normally takes a plural adjective:
With things and other non-human plurals, everyday Southern Levantine Arabic is more flexible. You will often hear a feminine singular adjective, even though the noun itself is plural:

You may also hear plural agreement in everyday speech. For now, do not try to force one rule onto every non-human plural. First, learn the basic pattern for human plurals, then pay attention to the non-human plural patterns as they appear in this chapter.

blocks.heading: Practicing the WDGN System
paragraphs: Do not try to master all four pieces at once.
Start with one.
If you are practicing Word Order, focus only on putting the noun before the adjective:
big house → bēt kbīr
Then practice Definiteness:
the big house → il-bēt il-kbīr
Then Gender:
a new car → sayyāra jdīde
Then Number:
nice students → ṭullāb laṭīfīn
Once each piece feels comfortable, start combining them.

The goal is not to stand there mentally saying W-D-G-N every time you speak Arabic. WDGN is a training tool. With enough repetition, you should eventually stop thinking about the checklist because the correct patterns will simply sound right.

blocks.heading: 2.3 A First Look at Plurals
paragraphs: Throughout this book, you have already encountered some plural words mixed into the vocabulary and examples.

Arabic has several ways to form plurals, including many broken plurals, where the internal pattern of the word changes rather than simply taking an ending. In Volume Two, we will take a much closer look at noun plurals, including the patterns that help you recognize and form many broken plurals.

For now, you do not need to learn the entire plural system. We are simply building some of the framework you need to get started. You will learn plural forms with your vocabulary while becoming familiar with two very common endings that you will hear again and again.
Learning these patterns early also helps you get used to the rhythm of Arabic—the “beat” of how words change when we talk about more than one person or thing.

blocks.heading: The ـين (-īn) Plural
paragraphs: You have already seen ـين (-īn) with nationalities and nisba adjectives. This ending is especially important when adjectives describe masculine or mixed groups of people.

Not all adjectives form their plural with ـين (-īn). Some use broken plurals, where the word changes internally rather than simply taking an ending. Later in this series, you will learn common broken-plural forms of adjectives and practice using them to describe groups of people. But for now, let’s get used to this pattern.

blocks.heading: Be Careful with Nouns
paragraphs: ـين (-īn) is not a universal way to make a human noun plural. Many common nouns have their own plural forms:

This is why the vocabulary banks in this book give you the plural along with the singular. For now, learn the plural with the noun rather than trying to guess it, and get familiar with the rhythm. In Volume Two, we will unpack the system behind many of these forms.

blocks.heading: The Key Pattern
blocks.text:
When an adjective describes a masculine or mixed group of people, ـين (-īn) is a very common plural ending:
طُلّاب لَطيفين | nice students – ṭullāb laṭīfīn

blocks.heading: The ـات (-āt) Plural
paragraphs: The ending ـات (-āt) is one of the most common ways to form the plural of a feminine noun, especially when the singular ends in tāʾ marbūṭa (ة).
However, this is not a universal rule. Many feminine nouns form their plural in other ways, so you should continue learning the plural together with each new noun.
You may also see ـات with nouns that do not end in ة:
That said, not every feminine noun uses ـات. Some common feminine nouns ending in ة have a different plural form:

items.en: pair of shoes → pairs of shoes

paragraphs: This is why the vocabulary banks in this book give you the plural along with the singular. Learn the plural with the noun rather than trying to guess it.

blocks.heading: Female Adjectives
paragraphs: ـات can also appear on adjectives describing an all-female group:
In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, you will also commonly hear ـين (-īn) with adjectives describing groups of people, including all-female groups:
Both are common and totally normal. For now, simply recognize both patterns. We will return to plural adjective agreement as you build more complex phrases.

blocks.text:
For many feminine nouns:
ـة ←  ـات
But this is a common pattern, not a universal rule. Learn each noun together with its plural.

blocks.heading: A Note on Broken Plurals
paragraphs: The patterns you have just learned are common, but Arabic also has many broken plurals. Instead of simply adding an ending, the internal pattern of the word changes.
Even a feminine noun ending in ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) may have a broken plural:
You do not need to master these patterns yet. For now, learn each noun together with its plural and start noticing how these forms sound.
As you keep reading, listening, and saying everything out loud, the patterns will begin to feel more familiar. Repetition is your friend.
In Volume Two, we will return to noun plurals and learn how many of these broken-plural patterns work more systematically.

lessons.title: The Nominal Sentence — il-jumle il-ismiyye | الجملة الاسمية

blocks.heading: What Is a Nominal Sentence?
paragraphs: Before looking at Arabic, it helps to begin with a familiar idea from English grammar. In school, students learn that a sentence has two main parts: a subject and a predicate. The subject is what the sentence is about, and the predicate tells us something about that subject.

For example, in the sentence “The car is fast,” the car is the subject, and is fast is the predicate. In that sense, English also has this kind of sentence: a sentence built around a subject and a predicate, rather than around an action.

In Arabic, this is called الجُمْلِة الاِسْمِيّة (il-jumle il-ismiyye), or the nominal sentence. At its most basic level, a nominal sentence begins with a noun or pronoun and then gives information about it. Like English, it has a subject and a predicate. Unlike English, however, Arabic does not need a present-tense verb like “is” to connect them.
So where English says “The house is big,” Arabic simply says:
There is no separate word for is. The sentence is complete because the relationship between the two parts is understood through grammar and word order.

In traditional Arabic grammar, these two parts are called المُبْتَدَأ (il-mubtadaʾ) and الخَبَر (il-khabar). The mubtadaʾ is the subject, or the person or thing being talked about. The khabar is the predicate, or the information given about the subject. If you keep the simple idea of subject + predicate in mind, Arabic nominal sentences become much easier to understand.

blocks.heading: Building Sentences
paragraphs: A nominal sentence in Arabic is not simply a fixed pattern like noun + adjective. More fundamentally, it consists of:
Subject + Predicate

The subject is usually a noun or pronoun, while the predicate is what tells us something about that subject. Although the predicate can take several different forms, we’ll begin with the most common one.

blocks.heading: The Most Common Pattern
paragraphs: Definite Noun + Indefinite Adjective = Sentence
This is one of the most common and useful nominal-sentence patterns for beginners:

Notice that the adjective does not have الـ. That’s because it isn’t identifying which house or which food—it is telling us something new about the subject. In other words, it functions as the predicate.
Pretty easy, right? Arabic is remarkably efficient.
Before we move on, though, we need to clear up one important point. There is another pattern that looks almost identical but means something very different.

blocks.heading: Phrase vs. Sentence (The Key Difference)
paragraphs: Compare these two examples:
Definite Noun + Definite Adjective = Phrase (Naming)
This is not a complete sentence. It simply names or identifies a particular house.
Definite Noun + Indefinite Adjective = Sentence (Complete Idea)
This is a complete sentence. It tells us something new about the house.

blocks.heading: The Rule
blocks.text:
When the adjective is part of a definite noun phrase, it must also be definite.
In the descriptive sentences practiced here, the predicate adjective is indefinite and does not take الـ.
This distinction allows you to recognize the difference between describing a noun and making a statement about it.

blocks.heading: Two Adjectives
paragraphs: Here are the two patterns you have just seen:
Definite noun + indefinite adjective = sentence
Definite noun + definite adjective = phrase
But what if you want to do both? What if you want to describe the subject first, and then say something new about it?
This is very common in Arabic nominal sentences. You can describe the noun with one adjective as part of the subject, then add a second word as the predicate — new information about that subject.

The first adjective stays attached to the noun and takes الـ (il-) because it belongs to the noun phrase. In the adjective-predicate patterns practiced here, the predicate adjective gives new information about the subject, so it remains indefinite.
Definite noun + definite adjective + indefinite predicate/adjective = sentence
The formula is:
Definite noun + definite adjective + indefinite predicate/adjective = sentence
Think of it this way: the subject arrives fully formed — noun and adjective both carrying الـ. The predicate travels light, because it carries the new information.

blocks.title: Nominal Sentence vs. Adjective Phrase
blocks.instructions:
Instructions: Fill in the blank with the correct adjective form. Pay attention to whether the English gives you an adjective phrase or a full nominal sentence.  In Arabic:
• Adjective phrase: The adjective agrees with the noun in definiteness.  Example: the big house → il-bēt il-kbīr | البيت الكبير
• Nominal sentence: The adjective is indefinite.  Example: The house is big. → il-bēt kbīr | البيت كبير  
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

flags.note: Drill prints اِمّ (kasra-hamza alif) while the answer key has إِمّ.

blocks.heading: Negation of the Nominal Sentence
paragraphs: Once you understand how the nominal sentence works in the affirmative, the next step is learning how to negate it.
In English, The house is big becomes negative by adding not: The house is not big. Because English uses the verb is, the negation attaches to that verb.
In Levantine Arabic, there is no present-tense verb like "is" to begin with. To make a nominal sentence negative, place مِش (mish) directly before the predicate. Nothing else changes.
Formula: subject + mish + predicate
That is the basic rule.

blocks.heading: Demonstratives and the Nominal Sentence
paragraphs: When you use a demonstrative like hāda or hāy, watch for الـ (il-) on the noun that follows. It changes the meaning.
With il-: “this house”
This is not a full sentence yet. It becomes the subject when you add a predicate. (Context and intonation can also make the same words mean “This is the house.”)
Without il-: “This is a house.”
This is a complete sentence. The demonstrative is the subject, and the noun is the predicate.

blocks.text: With il-, it’s “this house.” Without il-, it’s “This is a house.”

blocks.heading: Building on the Demonstrative Phrase
paragraphs: Once you have a demonstrative phrase — demonstrative + definite noun — you can extend it into a full sentence by adding a predicate. The demonstrative phrase becomes the subject, and the predicate adjective stays indefinite.
Formula: demonstrative + ال noun + indefinite  adjective = sentence
This is the same nominal sentence pattern you already know: subject + predicate. The only difference is that the subject is now a demonstrative phrase.

The WDGN rules still apply. The noun and its modifying adjective, if there is one, both take الـ (il-) because they belong to the definite subject. In these patterns, the predicate adjective gives new information, so it stays indefinite.

blocks.heading: Now add negation with mish:
paragraphs: To negate these sentences, simply place mish directly before the predicate. The structure stays the same — only the predicate is negated.
Formula: demonstrative + الـ + noun + mish + predicate

blocks.heading: And with adjectives inside the subject:

items.en: This big house is not expensive.
This new car is not cheap.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text: A demonstrative phrase becomes a full sentence when you add a predicate that tells us something about it. The noun and any adjective modifying it take الـ (il-), while the predicate adjective stays indefinite. To make the sentence negative, place mish directly before the predicate.

lessons.title: Basic Possession: The Attached Pronoun — iḍ-ḍamīr il-muttaṣil | الضمير المتصل

blocks.heading: 2.5 Basic Possession: The Attached Pronoun — iḍ-ḍamīr il-muttaṣil | الضمير المتصل
paragraphs: Up to this point, you’ve already seen possession appear in several parts of this chapter. Now we’re going to formally address it.

Possession is one of the most important grammar points in this book, and you’ll use it constantly. It also builds directly on something you’ve already learned: Levantine Arabic likes to keep things compact and let the grammar do the work.

In English, we use separate words like my, your, his, and her to show possession. In Levantine Arabic, possession is commonly expressed by attaching a short suffix directly to the noun. Think of it as a small tail added to the end of the word.
So instead of using two separate words for “my house,” the idea of “my” is built directly into the word “house.”
Using بَيْت (bēt – house) as our model:

items.note: Here, -ī means “my.” The house belongs to the speaker.
Here, -ak means “your” when talking to a man.
Here, -ik means “your” when talking to a woman.
Here, -kum means “your (plural),” talking to more than one person.

blocks.heading: A Simple Way to Remember the Endings
paragraphs: Instead of trying to memorize all these forms individually, notice three useful patterns.
1. Look for the -k sound in the possessive endings.
When the possessive suffix contains a k sound, it tells us that the noun belongs to the person or people we are speaking to.
Notice that all three endings contain the k sound, but the surrounding vowels and sounds tell us whether we're addressing a man, a woman, or a group.
For now, when you recognize these endings attached to a noun, think of the English word “your.”
This will help you identify possession more quickly without having to translate every part of the word separately.
2. Listen for the long -ī sound.
The long -ī sound is an easy one to remember: it sounds like the English word “me.” In these possessive endings, -ī is the “my” ending.
So when you hear that long -ī at the end of the noun, use the sound as your memory trick: -ī sounds like “me” → my.
3. Look for -na.
Anything ending in -na is a useful clue for possession. When -na attaches to a noun, it means “our.”
You may recognize a similar sound from إحنا (iḥna), meaning “we.” Remember that -na means “our” when attached to a noun.
The remaining endings are third-person forms. They all contain ه in Arabic spelling, but the H sound is not always pronounced. Compare bēto (his house), bētha  (her house), and bēthum (their house).
Notice that the masculine singular ending is pronounced -o in bēto, even though it is written with هـ in Arabic. The feminine and plural forms have the h sound: -ha and -hum.

blocks.heading: Feminine Nouns
paragraphs: Here’s an important point to keep track of: feminine nouns behave a little differently when possessed.
If a feminine noun ends in the -a / -e sound written with ة (tāʾ marbūṭa), that ending changes to t before a possessive suffix is added.
A helpful way to think about this is that the ة has a t sound underneath. When the word stands alone, it usually sounds like -a / -e. As soon as you add a possessive suffix, that hidden t comes back.
In other words, when the ة is put under pressure, it shows its true form: t.
Notice the extra i in shanṭito and ʾannīnitha. When three consonants would pile up, a short i often slips in to make the word easier to say.

blocks.heading: Possession and the Nominal Sentence
paragraphs: This fits naturally into the nominal sentence.
You already know how to say:

The structure is the same: subject first, predicate second. The difference is that the subject now has a possessive suffix. Remember that a noun with a possessive suffix is already definite. Just like البَيْت (the house), بَيْتي (my house) identifies a specific house.
For now, continue building sentences with a definite subject followed by an indefinite adjective that tells us something new about it.
This means you can take a noun from your vocabulary list, attach the appropriate possessive suffix, and immediately have a subject ready to build a sentence around.
Same structure every time. The possessed noun comes first as the subject, and the adjective or description follows as the predicate. No verb needed.

blocks.heading: A Note on Nouns Ending in a Long Vowel
paragraphs: So far, you've learned how to attach possessive suffixes to nouns like بَيْت (bēt).
However, some nouns end in a long vowel. When we attach a possessive suffix to one of these nouns, the pronunciation can change slightly.
Take كُرْسي (kursi), meaning chair.
Since this word already ends in a vowel (written with ي, and heard as a long ī once an ending is added), the possessive endings attach a little differently from the ones you've practiced with بَيْت.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
The possessive endings still express the same meanings.
The important difference is that the noun already ends in a vowel, so the endings do not always sound exactly the same as they do after consonants.
For now, focus on recognizing these forms rather than trying to memorize a new set of rules.
As you encounter more nouns ending in long vowels, these patterns will become easier to recognize.

blocks.heading: Putting It All Together
paragraphs: In this chapter, you learned how to start building real Arabic sentences using nouns, adjectives, simple nominal sentences, and possessive endings. These are the core building blocks that will help you understand and express yourself naturally in Jordanian colloquial Arabic.
Main Structures You Learned:
1. Noun + Adjective Phrases and Nominal Sentences

items.note: Indefinite noun + indefinite adjective = noun–adjective phrase
Definite noun + definite adjective = noun–adjective phrase
Definite noun + indefinite adjective = nominal sentence

paragraphs: Remember that possession also makes a noun definite.

items.note: Possessed noun + definite adjective = noun–adjective phrase
Possessed noun + indefinite adjective = nominal sentence

paragraphs: The important distinction is whether the adjective is part of the noun phrase or provides new information about the subject.
2. Demonstrative Sentences

On the next few pages, you will read a short dialogue between two characters that brings together many of the concepts you have learned in Chapter 2. Afterward, you'll complete a translation drill using that same conversation, this time without the English translation.
The goal is to see how much you can understand using the foundation you've already built.

Before you begin, a quick word: just like in Chapter 1, you are going to encounter some unfamiliar vocabulary and phrases in the story. This is intentional—some of it comes from the next chapter or two.

For now, do not worry about knowing every word. Your job is to use what you already know, pay attention to context, and trust your fundamentals. This skill is just as important as any grammar rule. Students who develop it early tend to progress the fastest.

blocks.title: “First Time at Ahmad's House”
blocks.context: Picture the scene: Sami is visiting Ahmad’s house for the first time. The two friends are about to go out for coffee, but before they leave, Ahmad invites Sami inside for a quick tour. As they look around, Sami notices a family picture, meets the family pets, and asks a few questions along the way.

lines.translit: ahlan w-sahlan yā Sāmi! tfaḍḍal, bētī bētak.
lines.en: Welcome, Sami! Come in—my house is your house.

lines.speaker: Sami
lines.en: Thank you. Your house is really nice.

lines.speaker: Ahmad
lines.ar: يسلم ذوقك. هاي غرفة القعدة. تفضّل.

lines.speaker: Sami

lessons.title: Dialogue Discussion: First Time at Ahmad’s House

blocks.heading: First Time at Ahmad’s House
paragraphs: Ahmad and Sami’s conversation is a good example of how much can happen during a simple visit to someone’s home. There are introductions, compliments, a few questions, and some expressions that you might not immediately understand from their literal translations.
Let’s look at a few of those.

blocks.heading: بَيْتي بَيْتَك — My house is your house
paragraphs: When Sami arrives, Ahmad welcomes him:

items.ar: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا يا سامي! تْفَضَّل، بَيْتي بَيْتَك.
items.translit: ahlan w-sahlan yā Sāmi! tfaḍḍal, bētī bētak.
items.en: Welcome, Sami! Come in—my house is your house.

paragraphs: بَيْتي بَيْتَك is a common expression of hospitality. Ahmad isn’t literally giving Sami ownership of his house. He’s making Sami feel welcome and comfortable.
Notice the possessive endings on بَيْتي and بَيْتَك. It’s a simple expression, but it uses grammar you’ve already practiced.

blocks.heading: يِسْلَم ذَوْقَك — That’s kind of you to say
paragraphs: After Sami compliments the house, Ahmad responds:
Literally, this expression refers to someone’s good taste. It’s a friendly way to respond when someone compliments something you own, your appearance, or something you’ve chosen.
You’ll hear it in situations where English speakers might simply say “Thank you.”

blocks.heading: هاي عيلْتي — This is my family
paragraphs: Sami notices a family picture and asks who the people are.
Ahmad responds:

items.ar: هاي عيلْتي. هاد أَبوي، وهاي إِمّي، وهاد أَخوي.
items.translit: hāy ʿēltī. hād abūy, w-hāy immī, w-hād akhūy.
items.en: This is my family. This is my father, this is my mother, and this is my brother.

paragraphs: This is a useful example of demonstratives and possessive forms working together.

Notice that Ahmad doesn’t need a verb meaning “is.” He simply points to each person and identifies them. Also, he uses the shortened colloquial هاد instead of هادا. As we discussed, there’s no change in meaning.

You’ll also notice that أَبوي and أَخوي don’t look exactly like the regular possessive forms you’ve practiced. These are common forms for “my father” and “my brother,” and you’ll encounter them again when we cover family vocabulary in more detail.

blocks.heading: A Few More Expressions
paragraphs: The second part of the conversation introduces Ahmad’s pets, Haru and Lulu. Sami is surprised by how big Haru is, and Ahmad explains that the dog is actually very calm.
There are a few useful expressions here.

blocks.heading: ما شاء الله — An Expression of Admiration
paragraphs: When Sami sees Haru, he says:

items.ar: ما شاء الله! كَلْبَك كْبير كْتير!
items.translit: mā shāʾ Allāh! kalbak kbīr ktīr!
items.en: Wow! Your dog is really big!

paragraphs: ما شاء الله is an extremely common expression used when admiring something or reacting positively to it. You might hear it when someone shows you a new house, introduces you to their child, or tells you about something they’re proud of.
Literally, it means something like “What God has willed.” In everyday conversation, however, it often functions as an expression of admiration or appreciation.

blocks.heading: شِكْلها غَريبة شْوَيّ — She looks a little funny
paragraphs: Ahmad describes Lulu by saying:

items.ar: شِكْلها غَريبة شْوَيّ… بَسّ هي كْتير لَطيفِة.
items.translit: shiklha gharībe shwayy… bass hiyye ktīr laṭīfe.
items.en: She looks a little funny… but she’s really sweet.

paragraphs: Here, شِكْلها introduces how something appears, while شْوَيّ softens the description.
Ahmad isn’t being particularly harsh about Lulu’s appearance. He’s making a lighthearted comment before adding something positive about her.
You’ll work more with these expressions in later chapters.

blocks.heading: ثَواني بَسّ — Just a few seconds
paragraphs: Before leaving, Ahmad steps into his room and says:
ثَواني literally means “seconds,” but it’s commonly used when asking someone to wait briefly. It is written with ث but said with s.
And بَسّ here means “just” or “only,” rather than “but.”
You’ll hear this expression constantly in everyday conversation.
